heading: 2 General Assumption and Symbol Explanation (2.1 General Assumption)
note: 40 and 41 are the chapter and sub-section headings and have no text of their own. 42 is the frame: the health evaluation of a medical check-up is taken as the analogy, and six assumptions follow. The framing sentence carries more weight than usual here, because the rest of the paper reuses the medical vocabulary literally (patient, diagnosis, treatment, physical examination report in the title). Assumption 1 (43) is a data-reliability claim, 2 (44) closes the indicator set, 3-4 (45-49) assert that the sample shares the population's distribution and that the population 'does not actually exist' - the self-contradiction is in the text, not in the reading. Assumption 6 (52-53) freezes some indicators under policy. 51 also carries the watermark line.

heading: 4.1.2 Select Health Range (80% quantile, K-S test, Q-Q plots, Table 3)
note: 124 defines the whole rule in one sentence: 80% of a complete system's countries are assumed healthy, so the 80% quantile of the sample is the estimator of the healthy boundary. 125-127 fix the three cases (positive indicators take the 80% quantile from the top as the lower bound, negative indicators from the bottom as the upper bound, 'others' get an interval from their fitted distribution). 128 routes the two 'other' indicators (GPI, employment rate) to a K-S test run in SPSS and, in the same block, disclaims the test's detail 'due to space limitations'. 129 checks: alpha = 0.05, both significance levels above it, both pass. 131 is the SPSS table read as an image-block and it shows GPI on 47 degrees of freedom while the employment rate uses 50 - three countries are silently missing for GPI. 130 and 132-136 are the Q-Q plots and their captions, read one by one. 137-140 are Table 3, the health ranges; three of its entries are indefensible as printed: government expenditure on tertiary education gets an upper bound of 100 and R&D expenditure an upper bound of 100, which are percentages of GDP and can never bind; 'Number of top 1000 universities per capita' gets no bound at all in either column, yet the indicator is scored in every OPG; and the column order in the extracted rows ('Education expenditure 100 1', 'School enrollment - 50 1.63e-6') no longer lines up, because the two bound columns overflow their cells.

heading: 4.1.3 Diagnosis of Health Conditions (OPG eq. 3, health classes, Figure 9)
note: 141 routes to a 0-1 acceptance model. 142 defines pi = 1 inside the range and 0 outside plus the weight omega_i; 143 states OPG = sum of omega_i pi over the fourteen indicators (eq. 3). 144 interprets OPG: only 1 proves complete health, a low value means at least one main indicator or many secondary ones are wrong. 145 announces the six classes and 146-153 define them: Healthy OPG = 1, Sub-healthy OPG >= 0.9, Unhealthy 0.6 <= OPG < 0.9, Extremely unhealthy 0.4 <= OPG < 0.6, Serious 0.2 <= OPG < 0.4, Bad OPG <= 0.2. heading: 4.2 Sustainability analysis with DEA-Malmquist model (4.2.1 Basic DEA model, 4.2.2 DEA-Malmquist model, 4.2.3 Sustainability analysis)
note: 157 routes to the CCR model by name and authority. 158 derives the efficiency ratio theta_j = sum_m y_mj u_mj / sum_n x_nj v_nj (eq. 4) and 159 defines the inputs, outputs and their weights; the index discipline is broken, since u_mj and v_nj carry the DMU subscript j that the ratio is supposed to be maximising over. 160-161 are the fractional-programming form (eq. 5) and its non-negativity constraints, and 161 again mixes indices: the constraint is written with y_mk u_mj, one DMU's output against another DMU's weight. 162 interprets theta = 1 as 'effective'. 163 routes to Malmquist because CCR 'ignores the temporal change of productivity', 164 reports that the year-on-year ratios come from DEAP and then states the sustainability criteria; the software is the only source of the numbers - no multiplier or distance function is printed. 165-170 give three criteria, each split two printed lines: three consecutive declines in the last five years means unsustainable, exactly two means poor, at most one means highly sustainable. 171 interprets the three scenarios in words, and its middle clause is the only hedge in the paper ('can sometimes maintain its current situation'). Note the window: the data are 2009-2018, ten years, but every criterion is phrased over 'the last five years'.

heading: 6.3 Treatment Plan: Our Targeted Policies (6.3.1 Declaration for Our Policies, 6.3.2 Policy Implementation Model Realized by Using Markov Chain, 6.3.3 Implementation Timeline for India)
note: 227 routes the plan and opens 6.3.1 with the '1. Short-term policies' label in its tail. 228 is the only mechanism block before the model: limited resources and economic pressure mean quality follows economic development, so the short-term package must be cheap. The three short-term policies follow as label plus body pairs (229-230 tuition and subsidy, 231-232 minimum wage, 233-234 admission standards for foreign students) and each body carries its own number, which is where the paper's only quantitative support for policy sits: education cost is 49.3% of GDP per capita across the 50 countries but 238.1% in India (a ratio that Table 3 caps at 0.54, so the two scales do not meet), an Indian GMTA requirement of about 710 is said to buy full waivers at '6-7 top American universities', and the minimum-wage claim rests on unnamed 'multiple research results in history'. 235 routes to the long-term package; 236 argues family planning from the observation that India's education and R&D expenditure are already above normal, 237 states the input-output-input feedback loop as the sustainability argument, 238 argues teacher supply from the educational environment. 239 is the tail of the 6.3.2 heading. 240-241 route the Markov model and declare it an assumption set. 242-254 are three assumption bullets, each split two or three printed lines, and they are the model's real content: three policy states (good, poor, counterproductive), next state depends on the current state and the current indicator value, and convergence to normal is asserted. 255 defines PIE, BU and DCN and points at Table 4; 256-259 are that table, whose three rows are read as images: X1 ~ N(k*DCN + 0.01, 0.01), Y1 ~ N(0.01, 0.01) for Good, X2 ~ N(k*DCN, 0.01), Y2 ~ N(0, 0.01) for Poor, X3 ~ N(k*DCN - 0.01, 0.01), Y3 ~ N(-0.01, 0.01) for Counterproductive - the second parameter is 0.01 in every row, so variance and mean-shift are written with the same number and the spread is never separated from the shift. 260 defines k and then classifies the realised X+Y: above 0.05 is good, below 0.05 is counterproductive, so the 'poor' state of the chain is unreachable and the equality case is unassigned. 261-262 derive the transfer value(i+1) = value(i) * (1 - (X+Y)) (eq. 6) and glue the 6.3.3 heading into 262's tail. The sign convention deserves a flag: a 'good' year has X+Y > 0.05, so the indicator is multiplied by less than 0.95, i.e. a good policy shrinks the value by at least 5% a year, while a counterproductive year shrinks it least. For an indicator that is above its health range that is the right direction and for one below range it is the wrong one, and the model has no term that knows which side of the range the indicator is on. 263 routes the timeline.264-270 read the three prediction figures (employment rate, enrolment rate, net flow ratio) and interpret their averages: 10 years to the employment bound, 13 years to normal enrolment, 48 years for the net-flow ratio. 271-272 are the timeline graphic's own labels (2018 start, 2028 and 2031 for the short-term pair, 2066 for the mid-term, 2118 for the target), 273 its caption, and 274-279 the sustainability timeline: 275 claims 'all our visions are achieved properly' straight from the plot, and Figure 20 puts the three stages at 2018-2033, 2033-2068 and 2068-2118, two years off the 2066 and 2118 printed in Figure 19. The 'number of higher education institutions' is admitted in 271 to be a discrete variable that Markov chains cannot project, so the long-term vision is the only one with no model behind it.

heading: 6.4 the Real-World Impacts and Difficulties
note: 280-281 route to the obstacles. Four numbered difficulties follow, each split two to five printed lines per block, and each one is a mechanism the model cannot represent: (1) elite education is expensive, so the government can only subsidise a few students and the predicted enrolment rise may not happen; (2) lowering the minimum wage hurts families that depend on odd jobs; (3) more students without more teachers lowers teacher retention, which then lowers enrolment - a negative feedback the Markov chain does not have; (4) the caste hierarchy survives the legal abolition, so low-caste students still do not get equal education. (4) also carries a stray 'A' citation marker in the running text ('dealing with social concepts.A Although'). Item (3) is the only place in the paper where a policy is argued to be self-defeating, and it contradicts the monotone convergence assumption of 242-254. 298 hands off with the optimistic close and glues the 'Model Strengths and Weaknesses' and '7.1 Strengths' headings into its tail. References start at 324 and run to 334 (13 items, wikipedia-heavy: items 3, 8, 9, 11, 12 are Wikipedia pages and 12 is the India article cited as [wiki-India] in the body); Appendix A runs 335-340 and holds the MATLAB AHP code (A.1, with the RI vector and the reciprocity check) and the Python Markov-chain code (A.2, whose visible constants are k = 0.0017 and normal = 77). Neither appendix carries a measured body paragraph of its own after 335, so they are described here rather than coded.

heading: 7 Model Strengths and Weaknesses (7.1 Strengths, 7.2 Weaknesses)
note: Four strength bullets and two weakness bullets, each label split from its body by the layout. Strengths claimed: clear health and sustainability criteria (300-303 argue that DEA-Malmquist captures quality change over time), enough indicators (six factors, fourteen indicators), DEA is 'completely objective' because weights come from the data, and Markov chains fit policy because next year's policy depends on this year's outcome. The objectivity claim needs the caveat the paper never gives: four of the six factor weights and every indicator weight in this paper come from an AHP judgment matrix, i.e. from the authors' pairwise opinions, so only the sustainability half is weight-free - and 308-312's claim that DEA needs no prior weights sits one section away from the matrix in 110. Weaknesses admitted: too few countries, so the 80% quantiles may deviate from the true distribution, and no drift in standards over time (2018 values are used for a 100-year projection). 316 carries the '7.2 Weaknesses' heading. 323 ends the paper's body and glues the 'References' heading into its tail.
